title: A cache simulator: splitting the address

prereqs.why: The whole of `decode` is this: which bits are the offset, which are the index, and what is left.
Each field is one shift and one mask, and the mask for a zero-width field is the case that catches people.
Three files are compiled separately and linked, so a signature that does not match its declaration is a link error rather than a compile error.

statement:
**Milestone 1 of 3.** A cache simulator, built one policy at a time.
This milestone is the address: how a cache takes one apart, and what a
direct-mapped cache does with the pieces.

### The files

```
include/cache.hpp   the interface. The public part is the contract;
                    the private part is yours to replace.
src/cache.cpp       where you work.
main.cpp            given, and read-only here: the driver.
```

The three are compiled separately and linked, the way a real build does
it — not pasted together. A diagnostic names the file it is in, and
clicking it opens that file at that line. Note the directories: the
driver includes `"include/cache.hpp"` and your source includes
`"../include/cache.hpp"`, because a quoted include is resolved against
the file doing the including.

### The geometry

A cache is a rectangle of lines: `sets` rows, `ways` lines per row,
`blockBytes` bytes in each line. `sets` and `blockBytes` are powers of
two, which is what makes the address split into three fields with
shifts and masks rather than with division:

```
 63                                  0
+---------------------+-------+------+
|         tag         | index |offset|
+---------------------+-------+------+
                       log2(sets)  log2(blockBytes)
```

`offset` picks the byte inside the line, `index` picks the set, and the
tag is everything above them — it is what has to be stored beside the
data so that two blocks landing in the same set can be told apart.

In this milestone there is exactly **one** way, so a set holds one line
and the index names it outright. There is nothing to choose between and
nothing to evict deliberately: a block arriving in an occupied set
simply replaces what was there.

### The commands

The first line is `<sets> <blockBytes>`. Every line after it is one
command. **Addresses are hexadecimal**, with or without an `0x` in
front, and the three fields are printed in hexadecimal too.

```
decode <addr>   print  tag=<t> index=<i> offset=<o>
read <addr>     print  hit  or  miss
stats           print  <hits> hits, <misses> misses
```

A line that is not one of these is ignored, and so is a malformed one.

### What the cache has to do

- `decode` splits the address for **this** geometry. With one set there
  are no index bits; with one byte per block there are no offset bits.
  Both happen in the tests.
- `access` reports whether the block was already present, and counts it.
  A miss brings the block in, so reading the same address twice gives
  `miss` then `hit`.
- Two addresses in the same block — same tag, same index, different
  offset — are the same block. The second one hits.
- Nothing is ever flushed, and there are no writes yet.

### The sample

```
4 16                     four sets of sixteen bytes
decode 0          ->     tag=0 index=0 offset=0
decode 1f         ->     tag=0 index=1 offset=f
decode 4c         ->     tag=1 index=0 offset=c
decode 1234       ->     tag=48 index=3 offset=4
read 0            ->     miss
read 4            ->     hit        same block as 0
read 40           ->     miss       set 0 again, but tag 1
read 0            ->     miss       tag 1 is sitting in it
stats             ->     1 hits, 3 misses
```

### How it is checked

Your `src/cache.cpp` is compiled against the given `main.cpp` and run on
the cases. Any implementation that behaves as described passes; the
private members in the header are a suggestion you are free to replace.

This is one milestone of three. Your files are carried forward to the
next one, so what you write here is what you build on.
hints: Start with `decode` and the `decode` lines of the sample. Until those four are right, nothing else can be: `access` is built on top of it.

`offsetBits_` and `indexBits_` are already worked out for you in the constructor. The offset is the low `offsetBits_` bits, the index is the next `indexBits_`, and the tag is `addr >> (offsetBits_ + indexBits_)`.

A mask of `n` low bits is `(1 << n) - 1` — but when `n` is 0 that is `1 - 1 = 0`, which is right, and when `n` is 64 the shift itself is undefined. Geometry `1 1` has both counts at zero, and it is in the tests.
`access` with one way is four lines: decode, look at `lines_[index]`, compare `valid` and `tag`, and on a miss overwrite both and count the miss.
